orbit_scenario.basis: Simulation-informed scenario, set by no config dial (the saturation curve's shell is computed at it): the project coverage simulation's 95 percent column reads 341 satellites at 450 km, 53 degrees, and a 25 degree elevation mask (investor-rounded to the 340 dial), and no polar candidate below 375 passed. Honest bounds (2026-07-14 audit): a fuller integer-phasing search finds 320 passing the same stored geographic metric, the saved 341 case is the robust one under equal-area weighting, the metric is geographic rather than population-weighted, the production minimum-search screens a single phasing family, and finite sampled periods do not prove continuous operational availability. 340 is a supported conservative scenario; the exact floor is an engineering decision.

iridium_physics.ecosystem_assumption: The Iridium model's phone-class tier assumes phone-form-factor devices with in-chipset support for Iridium's 1616 to 1626.5 MHz L-band (0 dBi, no external antenna). A literally-unmodified 2026 phone receives nothing on this band: no phone has an L-band MSS radio and the band is not a deployed 3GPP NTN band (COMM-668 / COMM-669 / COMM-670). Today's real in-chipset path on this band is Project Stardust (NB-IoT NTN): messaging and IoT, kbps-class, no voice (COMM-661 to COMM-676). The phone class's data-grade service (its own usage, a named constant) is therefore a forward assumption: a future where standard chipsets include the band grown up from the Stardust path, 0 dBi, no external antenna, at the cost of the low phone-class SE tier (a knowingly-taken capacity haircut of about 3x to 4x versus the gain terminals). Boosted-antenna devices are purpose-built (our hardware, no chipset assumption). The Iridium model is the MSS lane and never claims to reach an unmodified handset; the unmodified-phone lane stays on cellular spectrum (the High-Bandwidth Cellular Pure Play model).

the steady state, beyond the 10-year horizon

limits: Fluid (fractional) beams, idealized 3 dB footprints and one circular shell.
Residential (night-time) population, every place at its busy hour at once.
No terrain or building blockage, and no interference from other systems.
Take-up 1 is the maximal-demand bound: the capacity found is assumed used. The fluid model credits a beam hanging over a coast with its land share only (the coastal under-credit).
Computed with the band in full-time use (d = 1): the engine scales people and capacity by the downlink share d, and so ignores how d relaxes each cell's people cap inside the curve (ADR 008).
No interference trim for the directional classes: each terminal's own pattern suppresses the far-sidelobe leak.
The interference trim is a sampled mean: each row draws its victims afresh, so a step between two rows can be the draw's noise; the trim is read where it levels off, never row to row.
The directional terminals' pattern floor (-20 dB) is an estimate, optimistic for the small terminal.

Computed at the 25 m^2 reference panel. The engine scales the curve linearly by the scenario's panel over it (the panel rule). Below the reference panel every class carries at least what the rule gives, because a cell's people cap does not shrink with the panel: computed at 15.4 m^2 instead (one snapshot of the shipped grid, 342 to 40,000 satellites), the small terminal carries up to about 1.8 percent more capacity and people (2.0 percent more useful beams), the phone class up to about 1.1 percent more, and the mounted terminal exactly what the rule gives; each class's maximum use is up to about 4.6 percent above the rule's. Above the reference panel the people caps do not grow with the panel, so the rule gives at least what the panel would: computed at 40 m^2 (342 to 10,000 satellites), useful beams up to about 3.0 percent below the rule's and maximum use up to about 5.6 percent below (each the small terminal's), and the rule ignores the per-link SNR lift a larger panel also gives. Farther from the reference, as measured: at 10 m^2 the small terminal's gaps are wider than at 15.4 m^2 (its maximum use about 7.2 percent above the rule's), while the phone class's and the mounted terminal's equal those at 15.4 m^2 at the same fleets; at 60 m^2 every class's maximum use is further below the rule's than at 40 m^2, up to about 11.3 percent, and useful beams fall up to about 6.4 percent below (each the small terminal's). Each beam's rate is held at its reference-panel value: the link effect of another panel is not modeled.

A null marker is one the rows do not place: the saturation number when the elasticity of capacity is under 0.1 at no midpoint (saturation_not_reached_by then names the last midpoint, the geometric mean of the last two rows' fleets, rounded half up: the rows measure nothing past it); the crossing under 0.25 when the elasticity is under 0.25 at no midpoint; the fleet at which the useful beams reach 0.9 of maximum use when they are under it at every row. A supporting marker the rows cannot place before their first midpoint or row is null too, and a limit below names it; saturation_not_reached_by is null when the saturation number is placed.

assumptions: The Iridium model's phone-class tier assumes phone-form-factor devices with in-chipset support for Iridium's 1616 to 1626.5 MHz L-band (0 dBi, no external antenna). A literally-unmodified 2026 phone receives nothing on this band: no phone has an L-band MSS radio and the band is not a deployed 3GPP NTN band (COMM-668 / COMM-669 / COMM-670). Today's real in-chipset path on this band is Project Stardust (NB-IoT NTN): messaging and IoT, kbps-class, no voice (COMM-661 to COMM-676). The phone class's data-grade service (its own usage, a named constant) is therefore a forward assumption: a future where standard chipsets include the band grown up from the Stardust path, 0 dBi, no external antenna, at the cost of the low phone-class SE tier (a knowingly-taken capacity haircut of about 3x to 4x versus the gain terminals). Boosted-antenna devices are purpose-built (our hardware, no chipset assumption). The Iridium model is the MSS lane and never claims to reach an unmodified handset; the unmodified-phone lane stays on cellular spectrum (the High-Bandwidth Cellular Pure Play model).
Operations cost is assumed zero (0.0 USD millions per year): an explicit investor-instructed assumption, a fixed operations line to research and add later, stated here rather than silently omitted.

People come from the promoted saturation curve (saturation-v1), computed once with the band in full-time use at the 25 m^2 reference panel and the held 8 MHz: each class's people at a fleet are the curve's capacity there, times the downlink share d, times the panel factor, over the class's busy-hour load per person (its rate while active times its busy-hour share). Beams over oceans and empty land carry no one.

The reuse calibration is 0.15 Gbps per MHz per unit of spectral efficiency at the 25 m^2 reference panel, an estimate (COMM-410, COMM-411): it sets each class's satellite peak and the curve's beams per satellite.

The downlink share d is 0.67, the time-division duplex band's downlink time share (ADR 008): every people figure and every downlink capacity figure but the satellite's peak scales with it, and the uplink holds the rest of the frame, 1 - d. IoT's uplink, payload and single-tone rooms scale with 1 - d and its random-access room with neither, so an IoT class's capacity follows 1 - d while its payload or single-tone view binds and does not move with d while its random-access view binds.

The panel is 15.4 m^2, applied linearly on the curve: a panel factor of 0.616 on people, useful beams, capacity and maximum use, never on the saturation numbers, the ocean factor or satellites per launch. Below the reference panel every class carries at least what the rule gives, because a cell's people cap does not shrink with the panel: computed at 15.4 m^2 instead (one snapshot of the shipped grid, 342 to 40,000 satellites), the small terminal carries up to about 1.8 percent more capacity and people (2.0 percent more useful beams), the phone class up to about 1.1 percent more, and the mounted terminal exactly what the rule gives; each class's maximum use is up to about 4.6 percent above the rule's. Above the reference panel the people caps do not grow with the panel, so the rule gives at least what the panel would: computed at 40 m^2 (342 to 10,000 satellites), useful beams up to about 3.0 percent below the rule's and maximum use up to about 5.6 percent below (each the small terminal's), and the rule ignores the per-link SNR lift a larger panel also gives. Farther from the reference, as measured: at 10 m^2 the small terminal's gaps are wider than at 15.4 m^2 (its maximum use about 7.2 percent above the rule's), while the phone class's and the mounted terminal's equal those at 15.4 m^2 at the same fleets; at 60 m^2 every class's maximum use is further below the rule's than at 40 m^2, up to about 11.3 percent, and useful beams fall up to about 6.4 percent below (each the small terminal's). Each beam's rate is held at its reference-panel value: the link effect of another panel is not modeled.

The fleet is every comms launch the cadence share allows (100 percent of the Neutron cadence) times 16 satellites per launch, each cohort living 5 years: there is no fleet target and no cap, and no saturation number sizes, caps, stops or slows the build.

Satellites per launch is a direct scenario setting (bounds 1 to 16); this run flies 16. The validated counts are 16 with the Neutron block upgrade assumed from the first launch, for the stack kept in the fairing's cylinder at calculation C's pitch on a rod-held base (COMM-713), and 15 without the upgrade, the mass-bound count today (COMM-712).

Every seat is sold: each year each people class (the small terminal, the mounted terminal and the phone class) serves every person its living fleet carries, and each class's column is the whole fleet sold to that class alone, so revenue rises with the fleet.

Each class's price is held flat: the small terminal $10, the mounted terminal $50 and the phone class $15 a month. The phone class's floor is the investor's $15 a month, which no price haircut goes below. A lower price or a smaller market is a division in the conclusions, never in the model: a price haircut divides revenue only, a market haircut people and revenue, and every margin is re-derived against the same fleet cost, never divided or averaged.
Each class's own margin is its own revenue against the whole fleet's annualized build and launch cost (operations zero, above), null in a year with no revenue.

Each class's usage is the investor's (2026-10-04): the small terminal 2 Mbps while active, 2.5 percent of users at the busy hour and 0.5 percent off-peak; the mounted terminal 5 Mbps, 10 and 2 percent; the phone class 0.75 Mbps, 2.5 and 0.5 percent.

Spectral efficiency is estimate-tier: the small terminal's band 1.5 to 2.5, the mounted terminal's 2 to 3 and the phone class's 0.5 to 0.8 bps/Hz, each class read at its central value (2, 2.5 and 0.65).

IoT is two device classes, minimal-packet IoT and data IoT, carried on the phone class's useful beams (IoT devices are low gain, so their reuse follows the phone rule) in the uplink's share of the frame, 1 - d. Those are the beams lit over inhabited cells, the phone class's ocean factor of the fleet's beams (each reading publishes it), so IoT over oceans and empty land is not counted: a conservative basis. For every year and reading the model publishes the IoT room and each IoT class's device capacity alone at its engineering usage (minimal-packet IoT 48 messages of 340 bytes a day; data IoT 4 bursts of 100 KB a day beside 48 messages): the least of the payload-bits, random-access and single-tone-time views at their conservative ends, each class given the whole room, so the two capacities never add. A capacity is never a count sold and never revenue: IoT's customers, usage and revenue are the product case's (ADR 011).

The coverage floor (340 satellites) gates every sale: nothing is sold in a year whose living fleet is below it, and each IoT class's capacity is null there (IoT needs continuous coverage); from the first year at it every class is sold in full and both IoT capacities are published (a step with no phase-in).
Government is left out of revenue: the model carries no government count, price or line.

The readings: the coverage floor (340); 2,000 satellites, the retired cap, kept for comparison; the horizon-end full-cadence reach (the final year's living fleet, priced at the final year's annualized cost); and the steady state beyond the 10-year horizon (the final year's comms launches times satellites per launch times the life). The coverage floor, the retired cap and the steady state are priced at the final year's cost per satellite-year; a reading below the coverage floor sells nothing, and each IoT class's capacity there is null.

IoT's room, at each year's and each reading's phone-class useful beams L, the held width W (8 MHz), the phone class's central spectral efficiency SE (0.65) and the uplink's share 1 - d: the uplink bits a second, L x W x SE x (1 - d); the payload bits a second, those times a 20 percent MAC efficiency (COMM-659); the access attempts a second, L x a random-access window of 57 to 1,650 devices (COMM-654) x an assumed 1 window a second (no source gives a window rate); and the single-tone seconds a second, L x W over the 3.75 kHz NB-IoT tone (COMM-714) x (1 - d). Each IoT class's capacity reads each view at its conservative end: the payload bits after the MAC efficiency, the random-access window's low end (57) and the message airtime's high end (7 s of 4 to 7 s, COMM-719); the least, rounded down to whole devices, is the capacity, and its view binds (a tie goes to the earlier in that order).
IoT's room is the whole IoT uplink: no people class's own upload (the small terminal's, the mounted terminal's, or the phone class's on the beams IoT rides) is subtracted from it.
Each IoT class's capacity is read at its engineering usage, averaged over the day; the product case's devices sit at their own usage and time basis, so neither is divided by the other.

Each class's saturation number is a spectrum bound reported beside the launch cadence, never a build target or a cap. A fleet past a class's last computed row is refused, never extrapolated or clamped; so is a run whose final year's living fleet passes the fleet a class with no saturation number is not reached by, since the curve's rows do not measure the elasticity of capacity there and which limit binds is not known (ADR 005). The curve's stated limits are carried in saturation.limits.
The Iridium model is the MSS lane (owned L-band, purpose-built or in-chipset devices), never the cellular direct-to-cell unmodified-phone lane (the High-Bandwidth Cellular Pure Play model).
